name: The Cinderblock
description:
The Cinderblock occupies what was once a dense residential neighborhood on Chicago's near west side, a zone that experienced three separate corponation industrial fires in the 2140s and 2150s — two attributed to Axiom Industries chemical storage failures and one to what the official Palladian Group report called 'an uncontrolled energetic event' at a Palladian-contracted demolition site. None of the fires were fully suppressed. They burned into each other. The result was twenty-two blocks of structural scorching so severe that the buildings didn't collapse — they carbonized. The Cinderblock is a neighborhood of standing burned buildings, their walls intact but black, their interiors gutted, their windows hollow. It looks like a city that died upright.

In the three decades since the last fire, the Cinderblock has been recolonized. Not rebuilt — recolonized. People moved back into the carbonized structures because the Gray Zone was worse and the Cinderblock was free. They hung tarps where windows were. They ran extension cables from illegal taps on the Axiom substations that caused the original fires. They built markets in ground floors where the charring was shallow enough to be scraped away and the concrete still held. By 2200, roughly eight thousand people live in the Cinderblock, in structures that every structural survey says should not be occupied and that nobody is paying for structural surveys to actually condemn.

The ash is everywhere. It doesn't go away. It settles in hair and lungs and the food you cook and the water you drink, because the water filtration in the Cinderblock is inadequate and the ash is still leaching into groundwater from the deeper burn zones. Respiratory illness rates are the highest in GLMZ. Life expectancy in the Cinderblock is eleven years below the city median. The community health workers who operate the three informal clinics in the zone have submitted fourteen formal petitions to the GLMZ Municipal Authority requesting remediation funding. They have received three form-letter responses.

sights: Rows of carbonized buildings standing intact, their facades black and textured like charcoal, windows gaping
Colored tarps and salvaged panels providing color against the overwhelming gray-black — the only brightness in the zone
Ash drifting in the air on still days, visible as a fine gray haze
Ground-floor market stalls with scraped-clean concrete floors and careful, deliberate color — residents fighting the visual weight of the environment
Community murals painted on the least-damaged walls, bright and detailed and constantly being added to
sounds: Coughing — frequent, from multiple directions, the background sound of a sick community
Market noise from the ground floors: vendors, bargaining, children, the specific acoustic quality of sound in a roofless or half-roofed space
Wind moving through the hollow upper floors of carbonized buildings, producing low tonal notes
Ferrogate Security drones on perimeter passes, their rotors distinctive
smells: Ash and old carbon — decades old but still present, especially after rain
Cooking food, which smells slightly wrong because the ash gets into everything
The sharp chemical undertone of industrial fire residue in groundwater — detectable in anything boiled with local water
Antiseptic from the three community health clinics
atmosphere.feel:
The Cinderblock produces a specific kind of exhaustion in visitors that is not physical. It is the exhaustion of sustained injustice made visible and permanent. The burned buildings do not let you forget what happened here. They are the evidence, still standing, still black, still leaching into the water table. Residents have developed a complex relationship with this — some find the burned walls galvanizing, proof of what was done that cannot be demolished or redeveloped away. Others find it suffocating.

There is, underneath the exhaustion, something fierce. The community clinics are extraordinary. The murals are extraordinary. The mutual aid networks that keep eight thousand people fed and medicated in a zone that no corponation or municipal authority will meaningfully support are extraordinary. The Cinderblock is a place where people are surviving something that was done to them, and doing it together.

demographics: Predominantly Tier 1 and the Gray Zone-level residents, many of whom were displaced from other zones and settled here because it was the only place available. High proportion of elderly residents who were present during the original fires and chose not to leave. Significant population of community health workers, mutual aid organizers, and activist-journalists operating on minimal resources. A growing population of younger residents who were born here and have no other home to reference.
economy: Informal and mutual. Ground-floor markets trade in food, medication, and salvaged materials. The community health clinics operate on a combination of donation, barter, and sporadic grey-market pharmaceutical supply. Some residents earn Φ doing contract labor in adjacent zones — the Cinderblock is close enough to Axiom industrial sites that there is a grim irony in residents commuting to work for the company whose storage failures burned their homes. A small underground economy in ash-processed industrial byproducts, some of which have legitimate chemical value, provides additional income.
power_structure: The Block Council — informal, non-elected, composed of the longest-tenured residents and the heads of the three community clinics — coordinates mutual aid and external negotiations. There is no enforcement mechanism; the Block Council operates on moral authority alone. Ferrogate Security maintains a perimeter contract but does not operate inside the Cinderblock, a fact that is simultaneously a protection (no corponation security inside) and a vulnerability (no enforcement if something bad happens). Axiom Industries and Palladian Group both maintain legal teams whose primary function is ensuring the fire liability cases from the 2140s and 2150s remain unresolved.
dangers: Structural failure of carbonized buildings — the charring has compromised load-bearing elements throughout, and collapses occur without warning
Chronic ash and chemical exposure — the health effects are documented, ongoing, and cumulative
Axiom Industries periodically sending representatives to assess 'redevelopment potential,' which residents interpret correctly as precursor to displacement
Complete absence of emergency services — fire suppression, medical emergency response, and structural rescue do not reliably reach the Cinderblock
The deep burn zones in the zone's center, where the fires overlapped — structurally unstable, chemically active groundwater, and reportedly strange acoustic effects from the carbonized material
opportunities: The unresolved Axiom and Palladian fire liability cases contain evidence that has been suppressed — a lawyer or investigator who can access the sealed discovery files has leverage worth significant Φ
The Block Council will pay, in favors and information, for anyone who can document Axiom's current redevelopment assessment activities
The ash-processed industrial byproducts trade needs people who can move product discreetly into legitimate chemical markets
story_hooks: A structural survey team hired by Axiom Industries has been quietly working in the deep burn zones — not assessing buildings, but drilling core samples from the ground. A Cinderblock resident who works as a salvager caught them at it and followed one of the surveyors back to an Axiom subsidiary office. Whatever Axiom found in the ground during the fires, they want it back badly enough to be moving carefully instead of through the courts. The Block Council needs to know what it is before Axiom decides careful isn't working.

One of the community health clinic workers has been compiling a comprehensive health database for the Cinderblock — fifteen years of respiratory illness, cancer incidence, developmental effects in children — and is preparing to submit it as evidence in a renewed liability case. She has received two credible death threats in the past month. The Block Council has asked quietly for someone to keep her alive long enough to file, and to find out whether the threats are coming from Axiom, Palladian, or somewhere else entirely.
frequented_by: Cinderblock residents and Block Council members
Community health workers and mutual aid organizers
Legal researchers working the fire liability cases
Axiom Industries and Palladian Group representatives, operating with varying degrees of disclosure

notable_locations.name: Clinic Three
notable_locations.description: The largest of the three community health clinics, operating out of a carbonized school building with a carefully maintained interior — the best-resourced medical facility the Cinderblock has

notable_locations.name: The Deep Burn
notable_locations.description: The central zone where all three fires overlapped, structurally dangerous and chemically active — also where Axiom's survey team was drilling

notable_locations.name: The Mural Mile
notable_locations.description: A continuous stretch of community murals on the least-damaged exterior walls, documenting the fires, the community's history, and ongoing demands — a living monument and, practically, a Diaspora-accessible public art record
